project.objective: When and where did Anders Monsen marry Unna Halsteinsdatter, and what does the marriage record show?

questions.question: When and where did Anders Monsen marry Unna Halsteinsdatter?
questions.rationale: This is the central question of the research objective. Anders Monsen (LKFW-9XH) and Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX) are both present in the tree but no marriage date, place, or record has been identified. Norwegian church records (ministerialbooks/kirkebøker) and civil registration typically document marriage events with date, parish, names of parties, fathers, witnesses, and officiating minister — making the marriage record the primary source for all attributes the objective asks about. This is Priority 4 (objective not yet decomposed into sub-questions); since the objective is itself a single marriage event, the first question restates it with identifying detail.

exhaustive_declaration.justification: repository_breadth blocks: Digitalarkivet.no (Norway's national digital archives and the most comprehensive repository for Norwegian parish marriage registers, confirmed by the FamilySearch wiki Norway_Vital_Records and loc_001) and Ancestry collection 60606 (Norway Church Records, 1812-1938) remain unsearched. The volume_search finding that FamilySearch holds zero digitized marriage volumes for Hordaland/Hosanger 1810-1870 (log_113) does not convert these into inaccessible sources — it confirms that FamilySearch is not the authoritative repository for this material, which makes Digitalarkivet's unsearched state more significant, not less. Digitalarkivet holds the original Hosanger parish kirkebøker that FamilySearch lacks. The autonomous-mode operational constraint (inability to execute browser sessions) is not a record inaccessibility: Digitalarkivet is free and publicly accessible; Ancestry collection 60606 is accessible to subscribers. Neither is sealed by privacy law — the Norway_Vital_Records wiki confirms Norwegian marriage and banns records at Digitalarkivet are open to the public up to 2005. Skipping them for operational reasons does not satisfy the pursued-and-unavailable exception. Per framework guidance, when in doubt a gap is unsearched, not unobtainable. An interactive session must search Digitalarkivet (generated URL: https://www.digitalarkivet.no/en/search?firstName=Anders&lastName=Monsen&spouseFirstName=Unna&spouseLastName=Halsteinsdatter&eventType=marriage&from=1830&to=1870) and Ancestry collection 60606 (URL: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/60606/?name=Anders_Monsen&birth=1820&birthplace=Norway&spouse=Unna+Halsteinsdatter) before exhaustiveness can be considered. The RHD University of Tromso parish index (https://www.rhd.uit.no/bmd/bryllupsmappe_ENG.htx?fornavn=Anders&etternavn=Monsen&kjonn=m) is also a free, accessible, deferred lead.

stop_criteria.goal_alignment: FAILS. No convincing answer was obtained. The question asks when and where Anders Monsen married Unna Halsteinsdatter and what the marriage record shows. Every FamilySearch indexed search (collections 4237104 and 1468080, with all required name variants across 115 log entries) returned negative or non-matching results. All 41 female Halsteinsdatter brides indexed in the Hosanger area were reviewed and none is Unna/Urna/Udna. All three Anders Monsen entries in Hosanger batch M42128-3 were read and none marries a Halsteinsdatter bride. The question is entirely unanswered.
stop_criteria.repository_breadth: FAILS. This is the primary blocking criterion. FamilySearch collections 4237104 (Norway Church Books) and 1468080 (Norway Marriages) were comprehensively exhausted with all required name variants, and a volume_search confirmed FamilySearch holds zero digitized marriage volumes for Hordaland/Hosanger for 1810-1870 (log_113). Norwegian censuses for 1865, 1875, and 1891 were searched. However, Digitalarkivet.no — Norway's national digital archives, confirmed by the FamilySearch wiki (Norway_Vital_Records) as the holder of original scanned church registers including marriage registers open to the public through 2005 — was attempted via external_site tool but no capture was received (pli_009, log_049), making it functionally unsearched. Ancestry collection 60606 (Norway Church Records, 1812-1938) was likewise deferred with no search results received (pli_010, log_051). The RHD University of Tromso parish index was also deferred. These are accessible repositories; the operational constraint of autonomous mode does not convert them to unavailable sources. Breadth is not met.
stop_criteria.original_substitution: NOT APPLICABLE (vacuously met). No records of any kind were located through the searched repositories. No derivative-vs-original substitution question arose. This criterion cannot be meaningfully assessed against an empty evidence set.
stop_criteria.independent_verification: FAILS. Zero sources confirm the marriage. The question is unanswered; independent verification is not possible. The criterion requires at least two independent sources from different informants or record-creation processes — none has been found.
stop_criteria.evidence_class: FAILS. No records were obtained through any searched repository. There is no original record with primary information about this marriage in the project. The criterion requires at least one original record with primary information about the marriage event.
stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: MET (vacuously). No conflicting evidence was encountered because no evidence of any kind was found across 115 log entries. No unresolved conflicts exist in the project for q_001. This criterion passes only by virtue of the absence of any evidence.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: HIGH — blocks declaration. The FamilySearch wiki (Norway_Vital_Records) confirms civil registration in Norway began in 1876 for statistical purposes only and is not available for genealogy; the governing genealogical record type is the parish church marriage register (kirkebøk). The volume_search result (log_113) confirming FamilySearch holds zero digitized marriage volumes for Hordaland/Hosanger 1810-1870 means those registers exist at Digitalarkivet but have not been searched by this project. Digitalarkivet is identified in loc_001 as the most comprehensive free repository for Norwegian church records. The probability that the marriage — if it occurred in this area — appears in a Hosanger parish register accessible via Digitalarkivet is high. An unsearched, accessible, primary-holding repository of this significance means overturn risk is unacceptably high. The autonomous-mode deferral of Digitalarkivet and Ancestry is a search gap, not an inaccessibility.

items.rationale: The Norway, Church Books, 1797-1958 collection (FamilySearch ID 4237104) is the highest-priority search: 14.4 million records, 1.29 million images, name-indexed and free. Per loc_001, Norwegian marriages were recorded in the bride's home parish; since no specific parish is known for Unna Halsteinsdatter or Anders Monsen, this country-level indexed search is the most efficient first step. Search under both names and their variants: 'Anders'/'Ander'; 'Monsen'/'Monssen'/'Monsøn'; 'Unna'/'Una'/'Onna'; 'Halsteinsdatter'/'Halsteindatter'/'Halsteinsd.'. Per loc_001, marriage records after the 1830s include fathers' names and birthplaces of both parties — the image will show all content the objective requests about what the record shows.

The Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 collection (FamilySearch ID 1468080) is a dedicated marriage index compiled from different source extractions than the Church Books collection (ID 4237104), so it may surface records the Church Books search missed. Per loc_001, this is a legacy index-only collection — no images and incomplete — so any hit must be verified against the original parish register at Digitalarkivet. Search with the same name variants as pli_001. Run regardless of pli_001's outcome, since the index populations differ.

Digitalarkivet (https://digitalarkivet.no/) is the Norwegian national digital archives and the most comprehensive free repository for Norwegian church records, per loc_001. It often holds records not yet indexed on FamilySearch, including marriage registers (vigselsbok/kirkeboker). Search both the indexed database and, once a parish is identified from census results or the FamilySearch searches, browse the specific parish register directly. Also search the Norwegian Historical Data Centre (https://www.rhd.uit.no/indexeng.html), which provides a complementary parish-level index. This item should be executed via search-external-sites.

The Norway Census 1865 (FamilySearch ID 3756102, indexed + images) will establish the parish of residence of Anders Monsen and/or Unna Halsteinsdatter as of 1865. If the couple is already married, the census entry shows their household, children's ages (from which the marriage year can be estimated), and the parish — which is the parish to target for a marriage register search. If not yet married by 1865, individual entries will show where each resided, likely near the bride's home parish where the marriage would be registered. The 1865 census is the earliest mid-century population snapshot available with full images.

The Norway Census 1875 (FamilySearch ID 1529106, index only) provides a second population snapshot a decade after pli_004. If the couple was found in 1865, the 1875 census confirms their residence, household composition, and family growth — helping refine the marriage date estimate from the ages of children not present in 1865. If not found in 1865 (e.g., unmarried and in separate households), the 1875 census may show them together or still provide their parish of residence.

The Norway Census 1891 (FamilySearch ID 4067726, indexed + images) is the most detail-rich late-century snapshot and should confirm the couple's household, ages, parish, and all children. The identified parish from the 1891 census can be targeted directly in a browse of the parish marriage register at Digitalarkivet if the indexed searches (pli_001–pli_003) did not locate the marriage. Also supports identity confirmation across all three census years (1865, 1875, 1891) to ensure the correct Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter — an important check given the frequency of patronymic names in Norway (per loc_001: hundreds of men named 'Anders' with common patronymics in any given census).

If the indexed searches in pli_001 and pli_002 do not locate the marriage, execute a full-text co-occurrence search for 'Monsen' and 'Halsteinsdatter' (and variants: 'Halsteindatter', 'Halsteinsdtr') across the digitized Norwegian records corpus via the search-full-text skill. Norwegian parish marriage registers were handwritten in Dano-Norwegian; AI transcription of unindexed pages can surface entries that name-indexed searches miss due to spelling variation, partial indexing, or records not yet in the main index. Search as co-occurring terms (both required), unscoped to any specific collection, to maximize recall. Per record-type-guide.md, this is the highest-yield approach when indexed search stalls on an unindexed or partially indexed parish register.

The Norway, Church Books 1797-1958 (collection 4237104) was searched in pl_001 with givenName variants Unna, Urna, and Udna each combined with fatherGivenName=Halstein — all returned only noise. Per collection-quirks.md, the remaining required vowel substitution is 'Anna' (Unna → Urna → Udna → Anna). This is the last untried combination of the four mandated variants with the Halstein father filter in collection 4237104. Search: givenName=Anna, fatherGivenName=Halstein, sex=Female, recordType=marriage, collectionId=4237104, recordCountry=Norway.

Digitalarkivet (digitalarkivet.no) is Norway's national digital archives and the most comprehensive free repository for Norwegian parish registers, distinct from both FamilySearch indexed collections (4237104 and 1468080) and the legacy IGI extractions. It holds original scanned kirkeboker (church books) including marriage registers not yet fully indexed by FamilySearch. The RHD University of Tromsoo parish index (rhd.uit.no) provides a complementary free indexed search. Both were identified in the loc_001 locality survey. Deferred in pl_001/pli_003 due to autonomous-mode browser constraints; an interactive session is required to execute this search. Generated URL for interactive use: https://www.digitalarkivet.no/en/search?firstName=Anders&lastName=Monsen&spouseFirstName=Unna&spouseLastName=Halsteinsdatter&eventType=marriage&from=1830&to=1870 . Also search RHD: https://www.rhd.uit.no/bmd/bryllupsmappe_ENG.htx?fornavn=Anders&etternavn=Monsen&kjonn=m

Ancestry collection 60606 'Norway Church Records, 1812-1938' was identified in the curated external-links result (log_048) and confirmed in the exhaustiveness evaluation as an unsearched repository. This collection draws from extractions distinct from both FamilySearch's Norway Church Books (4237104) and the Norway Marriages legacy index (1468080), so it may hold the marriage record not surfaced by FamilySearch indexed searches. Requires Ancestry subscription and browser capture. URL: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/60606/?name=Anders_Monsen&birth=1820&birthplace=Norway&spouse=Unna+Halsteinsdatter

proof_summaries.narrative_markdown:
## Marriage of Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter — Not Proved (Search Incomplete)

### Research Question

When and where did Anders Monsen (FamilySearch tree person LKFW-9XH) marry Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX), and what does the marriage record show?

### Conclusion

The marriage of Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter has not been proved from the evidence gathered to date. No marriage record for this couple was located in any of the sources searched. This is not evidence that the marriage did not occur; rather, it reflects a gap in the repositories searched. The most probable explanation is that the relevant record exists in the Hosanger parish kirkebøk (church register) but has not yet been searched at Digitalarkivet.no, the authoritative Norwegian national digital archives. The question remains open pending those searches.

### Sources Searched and Results

**FamilySearch — Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958 (collection 4237104) and Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926 (collection 1468080)**

These two FamilySearch collections were queried exhaustively across 115 logged research actions. All name variant combinations prescribed by the locality guide for Hosanger/Hordaland were applied: the groom was searched as "Anders" and "Anders Monsen"; the bride was searched under the given-name variants Unna, Urna, Udna, Inna, and Anna combined with the surname variants Halsteinsdatter and Halsteinsdr. Zero results for the target couple were returned by any combination.

A volume search confirmed that FamilySearch holds **zero digitized marriage volumes** for Hosanger parish or the broader Hordaland county for the period 1800–1870. This is the structural explanation for the null results: FamilySearch does not hold the relevant registers. The locality guide (loc_001) confirms that collection 1468080 is a legacy index-only collection — incomplete, with no images — and that original scans of Norwegian parish marriage registers are held at Digitalarkivet.

As a check against the index gap, three "Anders Monsen" marriages recorded in Hosanger parish (FamilySearch batch M42128-3, collection 1468080) were located and read in full:
- Anders Monsen / Aubjor Nilsdr, 26 August 1849, Hosanger (record NW4C-DZT)
- Anders Monsen / Martha Johnsdr, 6 July 1851, Hosanger (record NW4C-DZB)
- Anders Monsen / Britha Olsdr, 19 May 1852, Hosanger (record NW4C-D8M)

None of these records involves a Halsteinsdatter bride. All three were eliminated.

All 41 female Halsteinsdatter brides indexed in the Hosanger/Hordaland area within collection 1468080 were individually reviewed. None is named Unna, Urna, or Udna. A fulltext search across all FamilySearch Norway records using the phrase "+Monsen +Halsteinsdatter" returned zero results.

**Norwegian censuses searched on FamilySearch**

The 1865, 1875, and 1891 Norwegian censuses were searched for corroborating information about the target couple. No census entries providing marriage date or place for Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter as a couple were obtained through the searched records. Census results are not a substitute for a marriage register but could have provided indirect evidence; none was found.

### Repositories Not Yet Searched (Deferred)

Three repositories identified during research have not been searched due to autonomous-mode operational constraints (inability to execute interactive browser sessions). These are not inaccessible sources — all three are publicly available:

1. **Digitalarkivet.no** (Norway's National Digital Archives) — the primary holder of original scanned Hosanger parish kirkebøker, including marriage registers, open to the public through 2005. This is the highest-priority next step. Suggested search URL: https://www.digitalarkivet.no/en/search?firstName=Anders&lastName=Monsen&spouseFirstName=Unna&spouseLastName=Halsteinsdatter&eventType=marriage&from=1830&to=1870

2. **Ancestry.com — Norway Church Records, 1812–1938 (collection 60606)** — a separate digitization of Norwegian church records that may cover Hosanger registers not on FamilySearch. Suggested search URL: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/60606/?name=Anders_Monsen&birth=1820&birthplace=Norway&spouse=Unna+Halsteinsdatter

3. **RHD University of Tromsø parish index** — a free Norwegian parish record index covering multiple counties. Suggested search URL: https://www.rhd.uit.no/bmd/bryllupsmappe_ENG.htx?fornavn=Anders&etternavn=Monsen&kjonn=m

Because these repositories remain unsearched, research exhaustiveness has not been declared, and the question is not resolved.

### Evidence Classification

No direct evidence of the marriage was obtained from any searched source. The FamilySearch negative search results constitute **negative evidence** — they demonstrate that the record is not present in those collections, which is informative given the volume_search confirmation that FamilySearch simply does not hold the Hosanger marriage registers for the relevant period. This negative evidence is derived from an index of secondary information; it is not a substitute for a search of the original registers.

### GPS Assessment

This conclusion does not meet the Genealogical Proof Standard:

- **Component 1 (Reasonably exhaustive research):** Not met. Digitalarkivet.no, Ancestry collection 60606, and the RHD index remain unsearched. These are the repositories most likely to hold the original Hosanger parish marriage register.
- **Component 2 (Complete citations):** Met for the repositories searched; citations are complete as documented above.
- **Component 3 (Analysis and correlation):** Partially met. The negative FamilySearch results have been analyzed and the structural gap (no digitized volumes for Hosanger) identified. No positive evidence exists to correlate.
- **Component 4 (Resolution of conflicting evidence):** Met vacuously — no conflicting evidence was found.
- **Component 5 (Soundly reasoned conclusion):** The conclusion that the record has not been found, and why, is soundly reasoned. A definitive conclusion about the marriage cannot be stated.

### Next Step

Search Digitalarkivet.no using the URL above, applying all relevant name variants. If no indexed result appears, browse the digitized Hosanger parish kirkebøk images directly for the estimated marriage period (approximately 1840–1870). Then search Ancestry collection 60606 and the RHD index. If the marriage record is located, re-invoke record-extraction and then proof-conclusion to update this summary.

jurisdictions.name: United Kingdoms of Sweden and Norway

quirks: The specific parish must be known to locate a marriage record — Norwegian church records are organized at the parish level, not nationally. Identify the parish before searching the kirkebøker.
Marriage was recorded in the bride's home parish. If Anders Monsen's parish is known but Unna Halsteinsdatter's is not, search for the marriage in each likely parish for the bride.

Patronymic naming: 'Monsen' means son of Mons; 'Halsteinsdatter' means daughter of Halstein. Surnames changed each generation. The suffix '-datter' is frequently abbreviated in records as 'd.', 'dr.', or 'dtr.'
Norwegian spelling was not standardized until 1917. Expect significant spelling variation in personal and place names across records — e.g. 'Unna' may appear as 'Una', 'Onna', etc.
The standard printed register format was introduced in 1814. Records after the 1830s typically include the fathers' names and birthplaces of both bride and groom — useful for identification.

Civil registration of marriages in Norway began in 1876 (law requiring data sent to the Central Bureau of Statistics), but this data is statistical only and not publicly available for genealogy. Church records (kirkebøker) are the primary genealogical source for all 19th-century Norwegian marriages.

The FamilySearch 'Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926' collection (ID 1468080) is a legacy index-only collection — incomplete, no images, and not being updated. Always verify any hit against the original record at Digitalarkivet (https://digitalarkivet.no/).

The FamilySearch 'Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958' collection (ID 4237104) has 14.4 million records and 1.29 million images with name-indexing — this is the best FamilySearch starting point for 19th-century Norwegian church marriages.

Farm names (gårdnavn) appear alongside personal names in Norwegian records and indicate place of residence, not a hereditary surname. Search with and without the farm name; a person may carry different farm names across their lifetime.

Records are written in Dano-Norwegian (Bokmål predecessor) and occasionally Latin for earlier entries. Consult the Norwegian Genealogical Word List at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norwegian_Genealogical_Word_List for key terms: viede/vigde/copulerede = married; ungkarl = bachelor; pige/jomfru = maiden; enkemand/enke = widower/widow.

Digitalarkivet (https://digitalarkivet.no/) is the national digital archives of Norway and holds the most comprehensive digitized collection of Norwegian church records, including marriages. It is free to access and often has images not yet on FamilySearch.
The Norwegian Historical Data Centre (https://www.rhd.uit.no/indexeng.html) provides an additional parish record search index covering multiple counties.
localities.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Norway — 19th-Century Marriage Research

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Period covered:** 1800–1900
- **Political status:** Norway was in a personal union with Denmark until 1814, then in the United Kingdoms of Sweden and Norway 1814–1905.
- **Administrative divisions:** Counties (*amt*, renamed *fylke* in 1917), subdivided into parishes (*prestegjeld* / *sokn*). Records were kept at the parish level by the Lutheran State Church.
- **Official language:** Dano-Norwegian (predecessor to Bokmål and Nynorsk); records may also include Latin terms.
- **Primary religion:** Lutheran (Church of Norway) — the state church kept virtually all vital records throughout the 19th century.

## Boundary changes
- The administrative unit *amt* was renamed *fylke* in 1917; county names also changed at that time. When searching pre-1917 records, use the older *amt* names.
- Place names changed after the 1862 and 1917 orthographic reforms (e.g., *c* → *k*, *aa* → *å*). A person recorded under one spelling may appear under another in later records.

## Available record types

### Church records (Kirkebøker) — PRIMARY SOURCE for 19th-century marriages
- **Denomination:** Lutheran State Church (Church of Norway)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (*fødte/døbte*), confirmations (*confirmerede*), marriages (*viede/vigde/copulerede*), burials (*døde/begravede*), moving records (*avgangslister/tilgangslister*), vaccination records
- **Coverage:** Nationwide from c.1688; standard printed format from 1814
- **What marriage records contain (post-1814):** Names of bride and groom, marriage date, ages, places of residence, marital status (bachelor/widower; maiden/widow), occupations, names of two bondsmen (witnesses). **After the 1830s:** fathers' names and birthplaces of both parties. Engagement/banns dates may also be recorded (three consecutive Sundays before the wedding).
- **Holding level:** Parish (prestegjeld) — must know the specific parish to search
- **Language:** Dano-Norwegian; some Latin terminology
- **Digitization (FamilySearch):** **Indexed + images** — Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958 (ID 4237104): 14,398,439 records, 1,288,153 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/4237104)
- **Digitization (Digitalarkivet):** **Indexed + images** — https://digitalarkivet.no/ — comprehensive free access; often has records not yet on FamilySearch

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** 1876 — a law that year required birth, death, and marriage data to be sent to the Central Bureau of Statistics (*Statistisk Sentralbyrå*)
- **Public availability:** This data is statistical only and generally NOT available for genealogical research
- **1915 Folkeregistre:** Community-level population registers started 1915, recording moves in/out; not publicly available in most cases
- **Conclusion:** For all 19th-century marriages, church records are the only genealogically useful source. Civil registration was not operational in a publicly accessible form before 1900 for most purposes.

### Census records
- **1801:** Nationwide nominative census — Indexed + images (FamilySearch ID 3733603; Ancestry; Digitalarkivet)
- **1865:** Nationwide nominative census — Indexed + images (FamilySearch ID 3756102; Ancestry; Digitalarkivet)
- **1870:** Partial census — Indexed + images (FamilySearch ID 4135961)
- **1875:** Nationwide census — Index only on FamilySearch (ID 1529106); Ancestry; Digitalarkivet
- **1891:** Nationwide census — Indexed + images (FamilySearch ID 4067726; Ancestry; MyHeritage; Digitalarkivet)
- **1900:** Nationwide census — Indexed + images (FamilySearch ID 3744863; Ancestry; MyHeritage; Digitalarkivet)
- **Value for marriage research:** A census taken shortly after the marriage will show the couple together; the age of the first child can help estimate the marriage year. Censuses also identify the parish of residence.

### Probate records (Skifte)
- **Coverage:** 1640–1903 index on FamilySearch (ID 1661306 — index only, no images)
- **Full records:** Digitalarkivet (https://digitalarkivet.no/content/115/rettergangsmateriale)
- **Value:** May name the spouse and surviving children; can help estimate the marriage date from the length of the marriage.

### Land records
- **Holdings:** Digitalarkivet (https://digitalarkivet.no/content/111/eiendom-og-tinglysing) — index + images
- **Value:** Farm ownership transfers may identify family relationships and residence.

### Farm books (Bygdebøker)
- Local histories organized by farm, tracing all families who lived on each named farm. Extremely useful for Norwegian genealogy. Coverage varies by county/municipality.
- FamilySearch Catalog holds many volumes; search https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog

### Military records
- Norway maintained military muster rolls (*manntall*) throughout the 19th century. Male census records often had a military purpose.
- Holdings at Digitalarkivet and the Norwegian National Archives (*Riksarkivet*).

### Cemetery records
- Norway Burial Index, DIS-Norge (1700–2010): https://slektogdata.no/gravminner — index only, free
- FindAGrave: https://findagrave.com — variable coverage
- Norway, Burials, 1666–1927 on FamilySearch (ID 1468081): 719,685 records, index only

### Immigration/emigration records
- Large-scale emigration from Norway to the United States began in the 1820s and peaked in the 1880s.
- Norway Emigration Registers, 1867–1973: MyHeritage (index + images)
- Norway Emigration Records, 1874–1960: Ancestry (index + images)
- Digitalarkivet emigration indexes: https://digitalarkivet.no/content/79/emigrasjon-og-flytting
- Norway Heritage emigrant ships: https://norwayheritage.com (index only, free)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Key collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Norway, Church Books 1797–1958 (ID 4237104) — indexed + images; Norway, Marriages 1660–1926 (ID 1468080) — index only (legacy); Censuses 1801–1900 | Free |
| Digitalarkivet | Full Norwegian church records (kirkebøker) index + images; emigration, probate, land, court records | Free |
| Ancestry | Norway Marriages 1660–1926; Baptisms, Burials; multiple census years | Subscription |
| MyHeritage | Norway Marriages, Baptisms, Burials 1634–1927; Census 1865–1910; Emigration 1867–1973 | Subscription |
| Norwegian Historical Data Centre (UiT) | Parish record search index | Free |

**Volume search coverage:** 5 digitized volumes matched marriage/religious marriage record types for Norway 1800–1900 in the FamilySearch Records Management Service (complete result set — no further pages). These cover specific parishes: Holte (Telemark, 2 volumes, 100% searchable), Fister (Rogaland), Rennesøy (Rogaland, 0% searchable), and Høle (Rogaland, 0% searchable). The main body of Norwegian marriage records sits within the indexed Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958 collection rather than standalone marriage volumes.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Digitalarkivet / Riksarkivet (National Archives) | Original church registers, probate, land, court | Free digital access via https://digitalarkivet.no/; in-person in Oslo |
| Regional State Archives (*Statsarkiv*) | Regional church registers and civil records | In-person or digital via Digitalarkivet |
| Local parish offices | Recent church registers (generally not public) | Contact individual parishes |
| Norwegian Historical Data Centre (UiT) | Digitized parish records | Online free |

## Records NOT online
- Not all Norwegian church registers have been digitized or microfilmed; the FamilySearch Wiki notes that "not all Norwegian marriage records have been microfilmed, and the beginning date of these records varies from place to place" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Marriage_Record_Search_Strategy_1814-Present)
- Community-level population registers (*Folkeregistre*, from 1915) are generally not publicly available
- Statistical civil registration data from 1876 onward is not generally available for genealogical research

## Research tips
- **Find the parish first.** Norwegian records are at the parish level. Use census records (1865, 1875, 1891) to identify the parish of residence of Anders Monsen or Unna Halsteinsdatter, then target the parish church books at Digitalarkivet or FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Getting_Started).
- **Search in the bride's parish.** Norwegian marriages were typically recorded in the bride's home parish, not the groom's. If Unna Halsteinsdatter's parish can be identified, that is where the marriage record most likely sits (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Church_Records).
- **Use the FamilySearch Norway, Church Books collection first** (ID 4237104) — it is the most comprehensive indexed+images collection on FamilySearch and covers 1797–1958 with 1.29 million images.
- **Cross-check at Digitalarkivet** — https://digitalarkivet.no/ is free, comprehensive, and often has records not yet reflected in FamilySearch indexing.
- **Patronymic naming:** 'Monsen' = son of Mons; 'Halsteinsdatter' = daughter of Halstein. Do not treat these as fixed family surnames across generations. The suffix '-datter' is commonly abbreviated 'd.', 'dr.', or 'dtr.' in the records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Naming_Customs).
- **After 1830s:** marriage records routinely include the fathers' names and birthplaces of both bride and groom. This is invaluable for confirming identity and identifying the next generation back (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Church_Records).
- **Language:** Records are in Dano-Norwegian; key marriage terms: *viede/vigde/copulerede* = married; *ungkarl* = bachelor; *enkemand* = widower; *pige/jomfru* = maiden; *enke* = widow. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norwegian_Genealogical_Word_List
- **Legacy marriage index:** The FamilySearch 'Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926' (ID 1468080) is a legacy index-only collection — incomplete and no images. Any hit should be verified against the original parish register at Digitalarkivet (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway,_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records).
- **Spelling variation:** Norwegian spelling was unstandardized until 1917; names like 'Unna' or 'Halstein' may appear in multiple forms. Search with wildcards or variant spellings.
- **Farm names:** A person identified as e.g. 'Anders Monsen Bakke' — the 'Bakke' is the farm name (place of residence), not a hereditary surname. It changes if they move farms.
